description: Recursively validate all JSON files in a directory and report syntax errors with file and line numbers.
thought_process: Found repeated complaints on r/webdev and r/node about cryptic JSON.parse errors giving no file or line context. jsonlint solves this but has dependencies and only takes a single file — no popular zero-dep CLI covers recursive project-wide JSON validation with CI-friendly exit codes, which is what teams actually need.
problem: When a JSON config or data file has a syntax error, JSON.parse tells you it failed but not which file or line — you end up opening files one by one to find the typo.
solution: json-check walks your project recursively, parses every .json file, and prints a pass/fail report with exact file path and line number of each error — exiting non-zero so it can gate CI or pre-commit hooks.
method: Pure Node.js, zero dependencies. Uses fs.readdirSync to walk directories, JSON.parse for validation, and parses V8's error message to extract the character position and convert it to a line number.

description: Scan your package.json dependencies for packages that haven't been updated in a while — spot potentially abandoned npm packages instantly.
thought_process: Found this pain point in r/node where developers shared frustration about zombie packages that show 0 vulnerabilities but haven't been touched in years. npm outdated only compares installed version to latest, not whether the latest itself is ancient. Existing tools like npm-check have dependencies. A pure fetch-based zero-dep solution fills that gap.
problem: Developers often don't realize their project dependencies have been abandoned — npm outdated shows version lag but not how long ago a package was last published, leaving stale and potentially vulnerable packages silently lurking in codebases.
solution: stale-deps reads your package.json, queries the npm registry for each package's last publish date, and flags any package that hasn't been updated in over a configurable number of days.
method: The tool reads package.json, then hits the npm registry's public JSON API (no auth, no dependencies) for each package to get its _npmPublishTime field, computes the age in days, and outputs a formatted table of stale packages sorted by staleness. Requests are batched 10 at a time.

description: Show when each of your npm dependencies was last published to spot abandoned packages
thought_process: Found this pain point across multiple HN threads and r/node posts where developers complained about inheriting projects with quietly abandoned dependencies. npm outdated tells you if you're behind the latest version, but it doesn't tell you if the package itself has gone dark. No popular zero-dep CLI fills this gap — existing tools like libyear require install and configuration. This tool runs as a one-shot npx command against any package.json.
problem: When you inherit a codebase, there's no quick way to see which dependencies haven't had a release in years. You only discover abandoned packages after they cause security or compatibility issues.
solution: dep-age reads your package.json and queries the npm registry for each dependency's last publish date, highlighting packages that haven't been updated in over a year.
method: Reads package.json, fires parallel HTTPS requests to registry.npmjs.org for each package, extracts the latest version's publish timestamp, and renders a colour-coded table sorted by staleness — oldest packages at the top.

description: Scan source files for leftover console.log, debugger, and TODO statements before you ship
thought_process: Dozens of dev.to and Medium posts in 2025-2026 confirm that console.log left in production is a persistent, frustrating problem. ESLint solves it but requires project-wide config and a full lint run; grep works but is stateless and requires piping. No zero-dep CLI fills the gap of a single npx command you can drop into any project or CI step for a quick pre-ship audit.
problem: Developers routinely ship debug artifacts — console.log, debugger keywords, and stale TODO comments — because grep is clunky and ESLint requires full project setup; there's no fast zero-config CLI that runs in any project and returns a CI-friendly exit code.
solution: dbg-scan recursively walks your source files, finds every console.log/debug/warn, debugger statement, and TODO/FIXME comment, and prints a color-coded report with file:line context — exiting non-zero when issues are found so it gates CI or pre-commit hooks.
method: Pure Node.js with no dependencies: uses fs.readdirSync to walk directories, regex matching against configurable patterns, ANSI color output, and process.exit(1) when violations are found — so it works as a pre-commit hook or CI step with no config files needed.

description: Spot missing, extra, and empty keys between .env and .env.example instantly
thought_process: Found repeated complaints on r/node and Stack Overflow about .env drift causing broken deploys. Existing solutions like dotenv-safe require code changes inside the app; no popular zero-dep CLI fills the gap of a simple pre-flight diff you can drop into any project or CI step.
problem: Developers routinely ship with missing or mismatched environment variables because there is no fast CLI way to compare .env against .env.example — you either inspect both files by hand or wire up dotenv-safe inside application code.
solution: envsync reads both files, computes a diff in milliseconds, and prints a color-coded report of missing keys, extra keys, and keys present but empty — with a non-zero exit code so it can gate CI or pre-commit hooks.
method: Pure Node.js with no dependencies: reads both files line-by-line, parses KEY=VALUE pairs while ignoring comments and blank lines, then computes set differences and emptiness checks, printing results with ANSI color codes.

name: env-diff
description: Compare two .env files and surface missing, added, or changed variables
problem: Developers switching environments or onboarding waste time manually comparing .env files to find missing or stale variables.
solution: env-diff reads any two .env files and prints a clear diff of added, removed, and changed keys with no dependencies.
method: Pure Node.js file parsing handling comments, quoted values, and export prefixes; outputs ANSI color-coded terminal diff.

name: gh-cost
description: GitHub Actions cost estimator — per-workflow breakdown, CSV export
